issue.title: websocket.receive_bytes() AssertionError
issue.body:
We have a FastApi/uvicorn websockets service.  During testing we can routinely (but not deterministically) trigger an AssertError from `websockets.receive_bytes()`:
```
Synchrony: 7.45: Synchrony.edge: Exception: AssertionError: error:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/app/synchrony.py", line 190, in edge
    if await call() is None: break
  File "/app/synchrony.py", line 170, in recv
    payload = await websocket.receive_bytes()
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.9/site-packages/starlette/websockets.py", line 89, in receive_bytes
    assert self.application_state == WebSocketState.CONNECTED
AssertionError
```
This happens (sometimes) during testing when we `$ kill <clientPID>` an active client that is using the service.  That is, when the connection to the service is abruptly terminated.  When we stand up the same service behind PyPi websockets we do not see such a failure.

For each connection there are multiple async tasks running.  Another task is doing `await websocket.close()`, which triggers a RuntimeError in deep in the starlette async close code, prior to (or concurrent with) the above failure.  Documentation is hard to find, so it's not clear that starlette websockets promise an idempotent close() method.  Nonetheless, AssertionError, by definition, means there's a code issue...

If there is interest I can post other (large) related stack traces.

Thanks.

```python
from typing import Optional, Dict, List

    def remove_empty(cls, values):

            if isinstance(value, dict) or isinstance(value, list):
                if not values[field]:
                    values.pop(field)
```

```python
from typing import Optional, Dict
from pydantic import BaseModel, root_validator

class Data(BaseModel):
    some: Dict

class EmptyDictTest(BaseModel):
    data: Optional[Data] = None

    @root_validator(pre=True)
    def remove_empty(cls, values):
        if values.get("data") == {}:
            values.pop("data")
        return values


EmptyDictTest.parse_obj({"data": {}})
```

issue.title: Custom 500 or Exception handlers do not run through middleware like other handled exceptions.
issue.body:
### Checklist

<!-- Please make sure you check all these items before submitting your bug report. -->

- [x] The bug is reproducible against the latest release and/or `master`.
- [x] There are no similar issues or pull requests to fix it yet.

### Describe the bug

<!-- A clear and concise description of what the bug is. -->

### To reproduce

```python
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.middleware import Middleware
from starlette.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from starlette.responses import JSONResponse

app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware)

async def not_found(request, exc):
    return JSONResponse(content={"error": 404}, status_code=exc.status_code)

async def server_error(request, exc):
    return JSONResponse(content={"error": 500}, status_code=exc.status_code)

exception_handlers = {
    404: not_found,
    500: server_error
}

middleware = [
    Middleware(CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=['*'])
]

app = Starlette(routes=routes, middleware=middleware, exception_handlers=exception_handlers)
```

### Expected behavior

both 404 and 500 errors will respond with their relevant json response, and correct CORS headers

### Actual behavior

the 404 error will response with correct CORS headers but the 500 error will not.

### Debugging material

Because `Exception` and `500` are special cased in `build_middleware_stack` any error bubbles up to the outer most `ServerErrorMiddleware` which is outside the other middleware, instead of being handled by the `ExceptionMiddleware` and passing through the custom middleware.

see: https://github.com/encode/starlette/blob/master/starlette/applications.py#L74-L77

I can see four possible fixes, none of them perfect...

- handle custom 500 errors in `ExceptionMiddleware` and prevent `ServerErrorMiddleware` showing its helpful debug info when a custom handler is present.
- have `ServerErrorMiddleware` run the response of the error handler through the middleware stack again, and if that fails resort to existing behaviour, adding a bunch of complexity.
- move the debuging info to a separate middleware and put that in front of the ErrorMiddleware, which would then cause it to trigger for every exception, but would allow `ExceptionMiddleware` handle 500s as expected, and `ServerErrorMiddleware` becomes a last resort.
- update https://www.starlette.io/exceptions/ to explain 500 errors are handled differently, and to get the above behaviour something like the following work-around is required:

  ```py
  @app.middleware("http")
  def exception_middleware(request, call_next)
      try:
          return await call_next(request)
      except Exception:
          return JSONResponse(content={"error": 500}, status_code=500))
  ```

### Environment

- OS: N/A
- Python version: N/A
- Starlette version: 0.13.6 and master branch

### Additional Context

#1116  seems to be have similar but refers to the generic `error_response` on `ServerErrorMiddleware`, this is similar but specifically about custom error handlers so i didn't want to hijack that issue.

Title: Custom 500 or Exception handlers do not run through middleware like other handled exceptions.

>  don't know about flask. How do they deal with this particular use-case?

@tomchristie flask separates middleware activities into a few different handlers (some are listed below). This enables flask first to run the error handlers, including the default "unhandled" case, and _then_ run response processing to e.g. add cors headers. Also, flask does have some magic to move `Exception` handlers to the end, but this is done via the custom `InternalServerError`(4) exception, which can be specified in `@app.errorhandler`(1) registration.

Starlette could potentially reverse this methodology to help out here. Would you be open to something like this?

```python
# starlette/exceptions.py

class InternalException(Exception):
    def __init__(self, original_exception: Exception):
        self.original_exception = original_exception

class ExceptionMiddleware:
    async def __call__(...) -> None:
       ...
        try:
            await self.app(scope, receive, sender)
        except Exception as exc:
            handler = None

            # existing handler lookup cases
            ...

            if handler is None:
                internal_exc = InternalException(exc)
                handler = self.lookup_exception_handler(internal_exc)
                if handler:
                    exc = internal_exc

            if handler is None:
                raise exc from None

# usage:
from starlette.exceptions import InternalException

def handle_unhandled(req: Request, exc: InternalException):
    record_metrics(exc=exc.original_exception)
    return JSONResponse(content={"error": 500}, status_code=500)

app = Starlette(...)
app.add_exception_handler(InternalException, handle_unhandled)
```


1. [`@app.errorhandler`](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.2.x/api/#flask.Flask.errorhandler)
2. [`@app.before_request`](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.2.x/api/#flask.Flask.before_request)
3. [`@app.after_request`](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/2.2.x/api/#flask.Flask.after_request)

Title: Custom 500 or Exception handlers do not run through middleware like other handled exceptions.

> So, if you _really_ want to do that, then wrap the middleware around the entire app...
> 
> ```python
> # Make sure the entire app is wrapped up in CORSMiddleware,
> # including 5xx error responses.
> app = Starlette(...)
> app = CORSMiddleware(app, ...)
> ```

This is _almost_ what we would like, yes. For middlewares such as [`asgi-correlation-id`](https://github.com/snok/asgi-correlation-id), you want them to always be run after any other exception handling has been done. Your approach require us to run `uvicorn` on the `CORSMiddleware` which wraps the `Starlette` app, which feels a bit weird.

The problem is essentially that the middleware stack looks like this:

```python
FastAPI.middleware_stack
-> ServerErrorMiddleware
  -> CorrelationIdMiddleware
    -> CorsMiddleware
```
and that the `ServerErrorMiddleware` overrides all headers. So now, any uncaught exception has all its headers stripped. For correlation (and sometimes CORS), we would want these headers to still be applied for uncaught errors. 

There's two solutions to the problem:
1. Allow `ServerErrorMiddleware` to be configured to keep headers
2. Allow us to explicitly pass in middlewares that will take the outermost middleware spots

The second option would allow us to build a middleware stack like this:
```python
FastAPI.middleware_stack
-> CorrelationIdMiddleware
  -> CORSMiddleware
    -> ServerErrorMiddleware
```

Since there is no way to do this nicely (but I'm happy to come with a PR if you accept one of the solutions), I've written a little util to patch this behavior, achieving option 2.

1. Install [`fastapi-stack-utils`](https://github.com/JonasKs/fastapi-stack-utils/tree/main) 
2. Add [patch_fastapi_middlewares](https://github.com/JonasKs/fastapi-stack-utils/blob/main/fastapi_stack_utils/middleware.py#L16-L60) _before_  `FastAPI`/`Starlette`, passing in the list of `Middleware()` you'd like to be further out than `ServerErrorMiddleware`.

```python 
from fastapi_stack_utils.middleware import patch_fastapi_middlewares
patch_fastapi_middlewares(  # this must be done _before_  FastAPI is initialized
    middlewares=[
        Middleware(
            CORSMiddleware,
            allow_credentials=True,
            allow_headers=['*'],
            allow_methods=['*'],
            allow_origins=['*'],
        ),
        Middleware(CorrelationIdMiddleware, header_name='Correlation-ID')
    ]
)
app = FastAPI(...)
```

```python

    resources: List[Resource]

```
And got the next error:
```
...
    raise validation_error
pydantic.error_wrappers.ValidationError: 2 validation errors for User
resources -> 0 -> roles
  field required (type=value_error.missing)
resources -> 2 -> roles
  field required (type=value_error.missing)
```
So, the reason of such error could be missing `roles` field, or it is equals to `None`.  

## Solution 1
You cloud make roles optional. Like this:
```python
class Resource(BaseModel):
    roles: Optional[List[str]]
```
It sets `roles` field to `None` even it is not provided at all.

## Solution 2 (Preferable)
I would recommend to use `default_factory` property like this:

We do not want the web server to couple an ever expanding set of pydantic models from our library of modules that feed into the message exchange. class HeaderDataModel(BaseModel):
```py
    class Header(BaseModel):
        src: str

    class Data(BaseModel):

        @classmethod
        def parse_obj(cls, *args, **kwargs):
            print('parse_obj() called!')
            return super().parse_obj(*args, **kwargs)

        def json(self, *args, **kwargs):
            print('json() called!')
            return super().json(*args, **kwargs)

    data: Data

    class Header(HeaderDataModel.Header):
        extra: str

    header: Header

    print(ModelA.parse_obj({'header': {'src': 'core', 'extra': 'test'}, 'data': {}}).json())
print('=' * 20)
print("Building ModelA.Data with {}")
print(ModelA.Data.parse_obj({}).json())
print('=' * 20)
print("Done")
```
Notice in the code snippet that `parse_obj()` accepts just `{}` for data when provided directly to the object but not when provided to an encapsulating model.  This is unexpected.  To further make this situation difficult, you cannot just override a method because they don't seem to be called recursively.  This, to me, is also unexpected.

Example code:
```py
import math
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class MyModel(BaseModel):
    myfloat: float = Field(..., lt=math.inf)
print(MyModel.schema())
# {'title': 'MyModel', 'type': 'object', 'properties': {'myfloat': {'title': 'Myfloat', 'exclusiveMaximum': inf, 'type': 'number'}}, 'required': ['myfloat']}
```

The `inf` is not json-compliant:

```json
{
  "properties": {
    "myfloat": {
      "exclusiveMaximum": inf,
      "title": "Myfloat",
      "type": "number"
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "myfloat"
  ],
  "title": "MyModel",
  "type": "object"
}
```

Note that the reason that I have `lt=math.inf` in the first place is because I am trying to limit myfloat to real-valued floats. Perhaps pydantic provides a better way to do this?

> 
> The status code provides a natural discriminator to use determine which model to use to deserialize a response, and so having one schema for a single response means it will be a lot easier to create a generated client that can deserialize your other possible error responses.
